cover.name: blood-moon
cover.title: Blood Moon
cover.caption: "Link... Be on your guard. Ganon's power grows...it rises to its peak under the hour of the [blood moon](https://zelda.fandom.com/wiki/Blood_Moon). By its glow, the aimless spirits of monsters that were slain in the name of the light return to flesh. Link...please be careful."

photos.name: fishin
photos.title: Gone Fishin'
photos.caption: Couldn't have asked for a better backdrop for my first foray into fly fishing. Allegedly the Merced river is a pretty good spot this time of year (for brown and rainbow trout), but we didn't have much luck. We did see some small fish further upstream later the next day, though.

photos.name: radagast
photos.title: Radagast
photos.caption: We did almost 30 miles in 2.5 days, with about 5000 ft of elevation gain. For me, that meant clutching to a walking stick for dear life basically the entire time, especially on the steep downhills. Each hike was well worth the effort though, and the only thing I'd change is remembering to bring both my braces instead of just one.

photos.name: smoky-2

photos.name: power
photos.title: Battersea Power Station
photos.caption: The hotel I stayed at in London was right across the street. I wouldn't recommend the hotel, but I would recommend stopping by the power station if you like architecture. Not really worth going inside since its a pretty standard mall these days, though.

photos.name: wes
photos.title: The Botanic Cottage
photos.caption: A quaint cottage found in the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh. I didn't get the shot quite right, needing to take it lower; but, you live and you learn.

photos.name: disappointment
photos.title: Historia and Eloquence
photos.caption: The overall monument is to William Ewart Gladstone, a prominent Scottish statesmen. Surrounding the state are virtues, 2 of which are pictured here. As far as I could tell, Eloquence is the one with the cone over their head. If whoever placed it knew that, I hope they recognize their comedic genius.

photos.name: horseman
photos.title: The Royal Scots Greys Monument
photos.caption: A memorial to the Royal Scots Greys cavalry regiment, commemorating those who fought and died in the Second Boer War and other conflicts.

photos.name: kid
photos.title: Robert Fergusson
photos.caption:
A prominent Scottish poet in the era of the Scottish Enlightenment. An excerpt from one of his most famous works on material vs. intellectual wealth, [Braid Claith](https://www.scottishpoetrylibrary.org.uk/poem/braid-claith/):

Ye wha are fain to hae your name
    Wrote in the bonny book of fame,
    Let merit nae pretension claim
        To laurel'd wreath,
    But hap ye weel, baith back and wame,
        In gude Braid Claith.

photos.name: poli
photos.title: Adam Smith
photos.caption: Statue to Adam Smith, a Scottish economist, philosopher, and the author of Wealth of Nations. I was surprised by the number of notable Scottish philosophers, and Edinburgh seemed to take significant pride in their country's intellectual history. Edinburgh is sometimes referred to as "the Athens of the North" because of this, and even tried to build their own full-scale replica of the Parthenon as a national monument. If you've ever seen it, you'll know to put emphasis on "tried".

photos.name: saint
photos.title: Sir Walter Scott
photos.caption: Sir Walter Scott, a Scottish author, is the subject of the Scott Monument in Edinburgh.

photos.name: seated
photos.title: James Clerk Maxwell
photos.caption: One of history's most influential physicists. I hear he had an [(electro)magnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Dynamical_Theory_of_the_Electromagnetic_Field) personality.

photos.name: swag
photos.title: James Braidwood
photos.caption: Allegedly, James Braidwood was the creator of the world's first municipal Fire Department.

photos.name: apostles
photos.title: The Holy Ghost
photos.caption: Likely a depiction of [Acts 2:4](https://www.biblegateway.com/verse/en/Acts%202%3A4), where a group was filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in tongues.

photos.name: flood
photos.title: The Flood
photos.caption: I'm not certain what is being depicted here, but there's definitely a religious figure guiding (or punishing?) a group of sailors. Some of the stained glass in Westminster Abbey is actually [quite modern](https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/explore-our-history/stained-glass), and I'd guess this falls into that category based on the richness of the cool colors, particularly the deep blues and purples.

photos.name: mixed
photos.title: The Battle of Britain Memorial Window
photos.caption: This is a fairly modern (1947) installment in the [RAF Chapel](https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/explore-our-history/raf-chapel) of Westminster Abbey. Something I found interesting in the UK was that stained glass memorializing those lost in battle, particularly in the World Wars, were fairly common (both in Scotland and England); I had previously only seen religious imagery depicted on holy grounds.

photos.name: renala
photos.title: Sir Charles and Sir John Wolfe Barry
photos.caption: There's something odd about seeing a king and a civil engineer enshrined in the [nave](https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/sir-charles-and-sir-john-wolfe-barry) of Westminster Abbey. Sir John Wolfe Barry designed multiple prominent bridges in the London area, including Blackfriars Bridge.

photos.name: demure
photos.title: Stained Glass
photos.caption: I don't remember exactly where this was; maybe somewhere in St John's Chapel? Definitely somewhere at the Tower of London.

photos.name: strategem
photos.title: Major-General Andrew Gilbert Wauchope
photos.caption: Taken at St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, in memory of a major-general who died in the Battle of Magersfontein in the Second Boer War. One of the more interesting pieces of Scottish history I learned while in Edinburgh is that much of England's military victories were paid for in Scottish blood. Its strange to see a monument to such an unjust conflict in a place like this.

photos.name: zealot
photos.title: Guardian of Scotland
photos.caption: This glass is from the oldest building on the Castle Edinburgh grounds: [St Margaret's Chapel](https://www.edinburghcastle.scot/see-and-do/highlights/st-margarets-chapel/). It depicts Sir William Wallace, one of the main leaders during the First War of Scottish Independence.

photos.name: cannons
photos.title: Tower of London Battlement Sign
photos.caption: Taken near the entrance of a tower along the battlements surrounding the property.

photos.name: castle
photos.title: Edinburgh Coat of Arms
photos.caption: I believe this is the Edinburgh Coat of Arms, engraved on an old police box. None of the police boxes in Edinburgh are actually in use by the force these days, with most being leased to micro cafes and such. This one had seen better days, and didn't seem to see any use.

photos.name: crest
photos.title: Scottish Achievement
photos.caption: Scottish coat of arms with heraldic achievement, at Castle Edinburgh.

photos.name: crunch
photos.title: Bronze 24-Pounder Cannon Heraldry
photos.caption: Likely a depiction of Satan, being consumed by 2 dragons. Ouch.

photos.name: dog
photos.title: Bronze 24-Pounder Cannon Maltese Quoin
photos.caption: The quoin used to support the barrel of this cannon is in the shape of a Maltese dog, a nod to its commissioners: the Order of St John (otherwise known as the Order of Malta).

photos.name: dragon
photos.title: Westminster Abbey Dragon
photos.caption: A dragon near Westminster Abbey's North Door. Where's [St. George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George#St._George_and_the_Dragon) when you need him?

photos.name: fence
photos.title: Fence [1]
photos.caption: Note much to say here, but I liked the ironwork.

photos.name: pulpit
photos.title: Preaching Tent
photos.caption: A preaching tent at the National Museum of Scotland. I liked the way the lighting was setup in the exhibit, and the texture of the wood. Outdoor services were particular popular in Scotland following the [Disruption of 1843](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disruption_of_1843), where ministers across the country broke away from the Church of Scotland. The Scots certainly were (are?) quite a cantankerous bunch.

photos.name: swords
photos.title: Fence [2]
photos.caption: Another fence with some nice ironwork, this one featuring some sort of stylized fleur-de-lis points.

photos.name: unicorn
photos.title: Unicorn Relief at the King's Gallery
photos.caption: Found on the door to the King's Gallery at the Palace of Holyroodhouse. Positioned across from the British Lion, the much less interesting National mascot of the UK countries.

photos.name: grate
photos.title: Bloody Mackenzie's Mausoleum
photos.caption: I didn't know what I was photographing until later, but this is a grate on the doors to one of the most famous graves in Greyfriar's Kirkyard: [Bloody Mackenzie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mackenzie_of_Rosehaugh) Mausoleum. He was a Scottish lawyer and prominent figure of the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters) that earned the name by being one of the its ruthless prosecutors.

photos.name: wheel
photos.title: Bronze 24-Pounder Cannon Wheel
photos.caption: Surely the cost of these wheels would have made even [Tim Cook blush](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mBHY_Qaw5AI).

photos.name: bee
photos.title: Cardoon
photos.caption: A bee visiting a cardoon ([cynara cardunculus](https://data.rbge.org.uk/search/livingcollection/?eti=Cynara+cardunculus&cfg=livcol.cfg&acc_num=&acc_num_qual=&barcode=)).

photos.name: bird
photos.title: Arthur's Roost
photos.caption: A bird seen near the ruins of St Anthony's Chapel on the way to the top of Arthur's Seat.

photos.name: buttercup
photos.title: St. John's Wort
photos.caption: At least I'm pretty sure this is some variant of St. John's Wart ([hypericum 'hidcote'](https://data.rbge.org.uk/search/livingcollection/?eti=Hypericum&cfg=livcol.cfg&acc_num=&acc_num_qual=&barcode=)). Its a surprisingly hardy plant, and depending on where it grows it has slightly different characteristics. The petals of these flowers are fairly broad, for example.

photos.name: pinky
photos.title: Codlins & Cream
photos.caption: Otherwise known as great willowherb ([epilobium hirsutum](https://data.rbge.org.uk/search/livingcollection/?eti=Epilobium+hirsutum&cfg=livcol.cfg&acc_num=&acc_num_qual=&barcode=)), but who'd use that name when "codlins and cream" is an option.

photos.name: fairies
photos.title: Mystic Water
photos.caption: A water feature at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh.

photos.name: bench
photos.title: Bench
photos.caption: A bench along the Water of Leith Walkway.

photos.name: lily
photos.title: Water Lily
photos.caption: A lone water lily in one of the ponds at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh.

photos.name: yellowflowers
photos.title: Ragwort
photos.caption: This is some kind of ragwort, which are members of the Daisy family. Possibly redstem ragwort ([senecio achilleifolius](https://data.rbge.org.uk/search/livingcollection/?eti=Senecio&cfg=livcol.cfg&acc_num=&acc_num_qual=&barcode=))? Its tough to tell.

photos.name: booba
photos.title: Displaced Finial
photos.caption: I believe this is a stone finial that would normally be atop some sort of gate or decorative pillar, but has broken off. The design may be of an acorn, which is representative of the cycle of rebirth.

photos.name: ded
photos.title: Momento Mori Stone
photos.caption: This headstone was off to the side, with no notable accompanying plaque or text. Since the kirkyard is thought to contain tens to hundreds of thousands of bodies, I took this as a marker to the less distinguished residents.

photos.title: James Harlay Monument
photos.caption: This one was tough to trace down, but it appears to be the grave of [James Harlay](https://fogk.org/2025/08/10/the-east-wall/). I can't find much about him, other than that he was "Keeper of His Majesties Privy Seal", which sounds... nevermind.

photos.name: headless
photos.title: This I'll Defend
photos.caption: This is the heraldic coat of arms of [Clan Macfarlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_MacFarlane), whose motto was "this I'll defend". The banner paired with the coat of arms' headless guardians is quite a statement on the inevitability of death and the futility of earthly squabbles.

photos.name: heads
photos.title: John Mylne III Memorial
photos.caption: It took some digging, but I believe this is the grave of [John Mylne III](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/75232661/john-mylne), Master Mason to the Crown of Scotland. I also believe these faces are some variation of [Green Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Man), foliaged figures meant to represent rebirth. Their somewhat grotesque appearance is likely also to ward off evil spirits from the burial grounds.

photos.title: Borthwick Monument
photos.caption: The most striking thing to me about the monuments and murals in Greyfriars Kirkyard was that so few seemed to depict religious imagery, instead showing memento mori symbols. Supposedly there are potentially hundreds or thousands of bodies on the grounds despite there being only 750 grave markers; so it makes sense that this would have started to feel like a Godless place at some point. This particular mural was in memory of James Borthwick, a famed surgeon, hence the depiction of various surgical instruments.

photos.name: hut
photos.title: St. George's Well
photos.caption: It's a shame to see something nearly as old as the United States vandalized, but the water from this well's spring is [notoriously foul tasting](https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=15325), so I guess its fitting that the exterior has been made to match.

photos.name: spooy
photos.title: The Foulis Memorial
photos.caption: A [monument](https://fogk.org/2025/07/11/the-foulis-memorial/) to the Laird of Ravelston and his wife, constructed by his son George Foulis of Ravelston.

photos.name: grave
photos.title: George Heriot Monument
photos.caption:
Although it can't really be deciphered now, the [inscription once read](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/85276703/george-heriot):

Passenger, who art wise, hence know whence you are,
what you are, and what you are to be,
Life, gate of death; Death, gate of life to me,
Sole death of death gives life eternally.
Therefore, whoever breathe draws from the air,
While live thou may'st, thyself for death prepare.

photos.title: Tenryu-ji Gate
photos.caption: One of the gates on the grounds of the [Tenryu-ji](https://www.tenryuji.com/en/) temple in Arashiyama.

photos.name: Spirit-Cat
photos.title: Neko
photos.caption: [Fushimi Inari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fushimi_Inari-taisha) is pretty polarizing if you look it up online, but I'd say it was well worth the time. I went in the evening, so it was much less busy and distinctly spookier (in a good way). Also, the shrine's many stray cats like to hide during the heat of the day, so you'll have a much better chance of spotting them later in the day.

photos.name: Tiny-Torii
photos.title: Tiny Torii
photos.caption: A tiny Torii spotted amongst the larger Torii at Fushimi Inari.

photos.name: Flute-Pimp
photos.title: Riding the Ox Home
photos.caption: Spotted in a small garden in Arashiyama, I believe this is a reference to one of the stages on the path to spiritual enlightenment. If this guy doesn't scream effortless peace, I don't know what does.

photos.name: Fresh-County
photos.title: Fresh County
photos.caption: As far as I could tell this was a sign for a local Kamakura [streetwear brand](https://freshcounty-kamakura.stores.jp/) called Fresh County, not a fruit supplier like I originally though 😅.

photos.name: Spooky-Grate
photos.title: Windows[1]
photos.caption: A close up of a building's window in [Shinjuku Gyoen](https://fng.or.jp/shinjuku/).

photos.name: Tokyo-Hotel
photos.title: Hoshinoya Tokyo
photos.caption: Staying at the [Hoshinoya](https://hoshinoresorts.com/en/hotels/hoshinoyatokyo/) in Tokyo was the best hotel experience I've ever had. The hotel was beautiful, the common spaces had free snacks and a cute daily activity, there was an onsite onsen (the only natural one in Tokyo!), and the staff was incredible. I can't recommend it enough, and have been dreaming of coming back since the day I left.

photos.caption: The Genji-ike pond at [Tsurugaoka Hachimangū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsurugaoka_Hachimangū), densely packed with lotus leaves at their summer peak.

photos.name: KIRIN
photos.title: KIRIN
photos.caption: In you've ever been to Japan, you'll know that they have an intense love of vending machines. These things are everywhere, even in unexpected places like outside this parking lot off the beaten path in Kamakura.

photos.name: Truck
photos.title: Torakku
photos.caption: Japan had lots of fun pint-sized vehicles. In particularly, I really enjoyed the trucks and utility vehicles, which felt more like scaled up Hot Wheels than scaled down American vehicles.

photos.name: Yearning
photos.title: Psyduck. My Beloved
photos.caption: The most expensive thing we did in Japan may have been trying to win this Psyduck plushie. Needless to say, we had to return home without it.

photos.name: Smokin-and-Drinkin
photos.title: Smokin' & Drinkin'
photos.caption: I'm not sure way, but I found this sign outside an izakaya near Shibuya(?) absolutely historical. So simple, yet profound.
